## Question 6

### Busiest Airports: Table #1

```{r tbl-passengers, fig.cap="Displays the average number of passengers passing through different airports (ATL, FRA, PKX) in different years (2020-2025)."}
library(tidyverse)

airports <- data.frame(
  airport = c("ATL","ATL","ATL","ATL","ATL","ATL",
              "FRA","FRA","FRA","FRA","FRA","FRA",
              "PKX","PKX","PKX","PKX","PKX","PKX"),
  
  year = rep(2020:2025, 6),
  
  passengers = c(
    42, 75, 93, 104, 108, 110,   # ATL
    18, 24, 48, 59, 70, 75,      # FRA
    16, 25, 35, 40, 45, 50,       # PKX
    28, 48, 65, 75, 85, 90,      # LAX
    25, 40, 60, 70, 80, 88,      # DXB
    30, 55, 70, 85, 95, 100      # HND
    )
  )

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

airport_table <- airports %>%
  group_by(airport, year) %>%
  summarise(passengers = mean(passengers), .groups = "drop") %>%
  complete(airport, year = 2020:2025) %>%  
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = passengers)

airport_table
```

## Question 7

### Busiest Airports Plot/Graph Figure #1

```{r fig-passengers, fig.cap="Passenger trends for major airports (2020–2025). ATL in red, FRA in green, and PKX in blue."}
airports_clean <- airports %>%
  group_by(airport, year) %>%
  summarise(passengers = mean(passengers), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(airports_clean, aes(x = year, y = passengers, color = airport, group = airport)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Passenger Trends for Major Airports (2020-2025)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Passengers (Millions)",
    color = "Airport"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Question 8

### Busiest Airports: Narrative Text

As shown in @fig-passengers, passenger traffic increased steadily for all three airports from 2020 to 2025. ATL consistently handled the highest volume of passengers, rising from 35 million in 2020 to 100 million in 2025. FRA and PKX also experienced substantial growth, with FRA slightly surpassing PKX after 2022. These trends suggest a strong recovery and expansion in air travel over this period, as also reflected in the values presented in @tbl-passengers.

## Question 9

### Monte Carlo Numeric Integration: Plot/Graph Figure #2

```{r fig-integration, fig.cap="The image features four scatter plots arranged in a 2x2 grid, depicting the estimation of an area under a curve for different sample sizes (n). Each plot contains a set of points, a curve, and a legend indicating the regions classified as above or below the curve."}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

monte_carlo_sim <- function(n, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, f) {
  x <- runif(n, xmin, xmax)
  y <- runif(n, ymin, ymax)
  y_func <- f(x)
  inside <- y <= y_func
  data.frame(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    y_func = y_func,
    inside = inside
  )
}

make_plot <- function(n) {

  df <- monte_carlo_sim(
    n = n,
    xmin = 0, xmax = 1,
    ymin = 0, ymax = 1.5,
    f = function(x) dbeta(x, shape1 = 1.5, shape2 = 1)
  ) %>%
    mutate(region = ifelse(inside, "below", "above"))

  area_box <- (1 - 0) * (1.5 - 0)
  estimate <- mean(df$inside) * area_box

  ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = region)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    stat_function(
      fun = dbeta,
      args = list(shape1 = 1.5, shape2 = 1),
      color = "black",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Monte Carlo Integration (n =", n, ")"),
      subtitle = paste("Estimated Area =", round(estimate, 4)),
      x = "x",
      y = "y",
      color = "Region"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plot10 <- make_plot(10)
plot100 <- make_plot(100)
plot1000 <- make_plot(1000)
plot10000 <- make_plot(10000)

plot10 + plot100 + plot1000 + plot10000
```

## Question 10

### Monte Carlo Integration: Narrative Text

@fig-integration shows four scatter plots of Monte Carlo integration with increasing sample sizes (n = 10, 100, 1000, 10000). Points are colored based on whether they fall above or below the curve, and the proportion below estimates the area. As n increases, the points more clearly fill the region and the estimated area becomes more accurate.

## Question 16:

### Self-Reflection:

I reflect on what I’ve learned so far in the course, especially with working with data in R. At first, I struggled a lot with pivot_longer()—I didn’t understand how to take the calcium dataset and turn all the different year columns into one “time” column. I would either get errors or my data would come out wrong with missing values. Now I understand that I need to specify the columns correctly and create new variables like time and group so the data is tidy. I also found making visualizations confusing at the beginning, especially in ggplot when I didn’t know what to put for aes() or why my graph wasn’t showing the right values. For example, I mixed up the x and y variables when trying to plot calcium levels over time, and my graph didn’t make sense. With more practice, I’ve gotten better at setting up graphs correctly and understanding what they show. Overall, I can see improvement from being confused about both data cleaning and plotting to feeling more comfortable doing both.
